analysis.one_liner: Ends the oil and gas industry's exemption from hazardous waste rules for drilling waste, produced water, and radioactive waste.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee from April 1992 until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Oil and gas drilling has long been exempt from the nation's hazardous waste rules, even though drilling leaves behind produced water (salty, chemical-laden water pumped up with the oil), drilling fluids, and naturally radioactive waste. This bill would have ended that exemption starting in 1994. It would have required permits and lined, monitored storage pits; banned spraying produced water on roads for dust control; barred discharge of produced water to streams without a strict permit; restricted selling contaminated land and equipment; set criminal penalties; made operators pay fees covering the cost of the permit programs; and required states to find and clean up old, unregulated waste sites. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near oil and gas wells — especially rural households that rely on groundwater — along with farms, ranches, and wildlife near waste pits. The bill targeted exactly the wastes that can leak into drinking water: produced water, drilling fluids, and radioactive scale from pipes and equipment [S2]. It also required a public database of contaminated sites and gave citizens a clearer right to sue over permit violations [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Beginning January 1, 1994, wastes from oil and gas exploration and production would become subject to hazardous waste management requirements under the Solid Waste Disposal Act, ending the long-standing exemption [S2].

Surface pits holding produced water would have to meet liner, leak-detection, and groundwater monitoring standards, and discharging produced water to streams would be barred after 1994 unless permitted with limits on organic, radioactive, and chloride constituents [S2].

States would have to identify, evaluate, and remediate unregulated waste sites — at least 10 percent evaluated each year starting four years after enactment — and EPA would build a publicly accessible database of them [S3].

The bill bans using produced water for dust suppression or road treatment, restricts transferring radium-contaminated land or overexposed equipment for unrestricted use, and adds criminal penalties for knowing violations involving drilling wastes [S2].

Owners and operators of permitted facilities would pay annual fees covering the full cost of administering and enforcing the permit program, with a 50 percent penalty plus interest for nonpayment, so taxpayers would not foot the bill [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would bear compliance costs: permits and fees, engineered storage pits with liners and monitoring, testing and record-keeping for drilling fluids, site surveys and cleanup of radioactive contamination, and financial assurances for closure and corrective action [S2] [S3]. Some of those costs would likely reach consumers at the pump, and the bill's later deadlines for low-production 'stripper' wells show it anticipated real strain on small operators [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, some small wells

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small, marginal 'stripper' wells; the bill itself acknowledged this by delaying pit-closure deadlines for stripper well properties until 1997, later than other wells [S3].

The permit and fee machinery is heavy: annual fees covering all program costs, biennial state reviews, extensive registration and record-keeping, and a state-run site-remediation program financed by fees on drilling and production [S3].
The bill singles out geothermal energy wastes for continued exemption unless EPA affirmatively finds regulation necessary, an inconsistency an honest supporter would have to defend [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is strong — drilling waste was the single largest waste stream exempt from hazardous waste rules, and it includes radioactive material and chemicals that reach groundwater. The costs are real and fall heavily on small operators, though the bill's own stripper-well phase-ins and fee-funded state programs show an attempt to spread them over time. On balance a genuine public-protection bill whose main design question is pace and burden, not whether the wastes deserve regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Transportation and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee, and died there when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Eckart of Ohio introduced the bill on April 9, 1992, with two Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 1, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, where the action history ends [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, who kept the exemption from hazardous waste regulation for drilling waste, produced water, and radioactive waste, and continued to operate under the far looser preexisting rules. Communities near drilling sites gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers, still exempt

for.name: Rep. Dennis E. Eckart
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or held action on it; the bill moved only as far as the Transportation and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee.

against.name: Oil and gas producers
against.role: Industry holding the regulatory exemption the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: The industry had successfully defended its exemption from hazardous waste rules since 1980 and opposed extending them to exploration and production waste; no such opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no party split on the merits is visible in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production
industries.note: The bill would end the industry's exemption from hazardous waste law for produced water, drilling fluids, and radioactive waste, imposing permits, fees, engineered storage, testing, and site cleanup [S2] [S3]. Its cost is the public's gain: these are the wastes that contaminate groundwater and expose people to radioactivity.

The bill exempts geothermal exploration and development wastes from the new hazardous waste requirements unless EPA finds regulation necessary, sparing geothermal operators the compliance costs their oil and gas counterparts would face [S2].

industries.industry: Environmental testing, engineering, and remediation firms
industries.note: Mandatory site identification, surveys, testing, and remediation of legacy waste sites would create demand for environmental engineering and cleanup services paid through fees on drilling and production [S3].
